entries.reason: It is the grader of the page's own practice-1, which builds the primary bitmap; the authored exercise reads both bitmaps instead, so no exercise is built from it.

It is the grader of the corpus's own practice-1 for this page, which decodes an MTI's four digits; the authored exercises practise request/response pairing and reversal instead, so no exercise is built from it.

It is a whole jPOS program that builds and prints a 0200 message with a GenericPackager loaded from iso87ascii.xml, a file the corpus does not ship; the page's subject is what ISO-8583 is and why it matters, so its one exercise is a quiz on that prose, and message building is practised on the later pages that teach it.
An ADVT scenario sent to an autowired handler of a Spring Boot application with a network-supplied EMV blob; the graded run has neither the application nor Visa's scripts.
A VGAT e-commerce scenario against the same autowired Spring Boot handler; it shows which fields such a request sets, not a step a reader can write offline.
An M-TIP scenario against the same autowired handler; it differs from the ADVT example only in the card and the EMV data.
A MIP authorisation scenario against the same autowired handler; the certification itself runs against Mastercard's network.
A directory tree; there is nothing to run.
Spring service wiring with an empty processing method and a live ISOServer; no behaviour of its own.
Spring MVC controller advice that logs and returns a fixed body; a graded run has no web layer.
A participant that logs at each lifecycle step; the logging habit is practised by the transaction-logging exercise and the lifecycle belongs to the transaction manager.
A GenericPackager subclass whose overrides are left empty and whose XML file does not exist; there is nothing to practise.
PooledConnectionFactory is not a jPOS class and the pool connects to a live host; a graded run has no peer.
Spring cache configuration around a method with no body; the idea of caching is named, not taught.
A Q2 channel adaptor that connects to a remote host over TLS; a graded run has no network and no peer.
Spring Security web configuration; a graded run has no Spring Security and no web layer.
A GDPR service whose methods have no body; there is nothing to practise.
A CCPA REST controller whose methods only return fixed strings; a graded run has no web layer.
A strategy map whose strategies have no body; it shows a design choice, not a behaviour to check.
It sets fields 22, 23 and 26 to example codes the page hedges as network-specific; there is no step beyond msg.set, which earlier pages practise.
Its field 48 layout is an illustrative private-use format that varies by network; reading length-marked values out of one field is practised on field 55 instead.
It repeats the length-prefixed layout of 14.3.1 in field 124 with three different identifiers; nothing new to practise.
The field-length validator of 15.1.2 checks a message against its definition, the habit the bitmap exercise already practises, so it is kept on the page and not practised twice.
It wires the two validators of 15.1 into a message processor and logs the failure; it has no step of its own beyond 15.1.1 and 15.1.2.
The timeout handler sends on a live NACChannel to a peer; a graded run has no network and no peer, so it cannot be the basis of an exercise that runs offline.
The retry mechanism wraps the live-channel timeout handler of 15.2.1 and sleeps five seconds between tries; a graded run has no network and no peer to retry against.
It sends each transaction through the retry mechanism of 15.2.2, so it needs the same live channel; a graded run has no network and no peer.
A sample 0200 written as JSON, shown for its shape; the page asks nothing of the reader about it.
The JSON channel depends on Jackson, which a graded run does not have, and is a sketch that would not work as written.
The same sample 0200 written as XML, shown for its shape; the page asks nothing of the reader about it.
It maps two fields into an ISO 20022 group header and leaves the rest as 'add more elements as needed'; the page's point, translating at the boundary, is asked through the gateway question.

entries.reason: It sets an MTI on an ISOMsg and prints it back; decoding the MTI's digits is the corpus's own graded MTI practice, so nothing new is left to practise here.
It checks fields with hasField and prints them; which fields are present is practised where a receiver actually learns it, from the bitmap, in the exercise built on section 2.2.
It prints an optional field when hasField says it is there; a single presence guard, with nothing to practise beyond what the message-structure page already does.
It reads fields of several data types off a message and splits track 2 at the equals sign; the data types are practised through their formats in encode-a-field, and the rest is printing.
The 0200 request is built with exactly the fields of the 0100 request in 4.1.1; it has nothing of its own to practise beyond match-the-response, which covers the 0200/0210 pair.
The 0210 handler is the 0110 handler of 4.1.2 with other words printed; reading field 39 is practised in match-the-response.
The echo test stamps field 7 and the STAN from the wall clock and only means something against a live peer; a graded run is offline and cannot rely on the clock.
The 0810 handler reads field 39 like the other handlers; reading field 39 is practised in match-the-response, which includes the 0800/0810 pair.
A switch that routes eight MTIs to empty handlers; there is no behaviour to check beyond reading the MTI, which match-the-response already does.
The data-element handler only wraps ISOMsg.set and getString for fields 48, 61 and 63; it has no decision of its own to practise.
The batch job is a scheduled wiring of a repository, a clearing-file generator and a settlement service the page never defines, and it reads the wall clock; nothing in it can be checked offline.
The chargeback service needs a transaction store and builds a reversal with a response code in its request, which is not a construction a practice should teach.
It tests the authorization service with Spring Boot's test runner and JUnit 4, which a graded run does not have; the exercise's own tests cover the same approved and declined answers.
The key manager rests on a key file on disk and on security-module methods that jPOS 2.1.7 does not have, so it cannot be the basis of an exercise that runs.
The MAC generator is one JCE HMAC call and a comparison; it leaves the reader no decision of their own to practise.
The DUKPT derivation is not the standard algorithm and has no published vector to check it against, so an exercise built on it would teach a wrong result.
